title: Production & Factor Prices
text:
\[Y = A\,K^{\alpha} L^{1-\alpha}\]

\(A\) = total factor productivity, \(K\) = capital, \(L\) = labor, \(\alpha\) = capital’s share.
Marginal products: \(MPL = (1-\alpha)\dfrac{Y}{L}\),   \(MPK = \alpha\dfrac{Y}{K}\).
Factor prices: real wage \(W/P = MPL\); real rental \(R/P = MPK\).
Income shares are constant: labor gets \((1-\alpha)Y\), capital gets \(\alpha Y\) — they add up to \(Y\) (Euler).







Try it. Add capital and watch the wage rise but the rental rate fall. Change \(\alpha\) to re-slice the pie between labor and capital.





 
  Productivity A: 1.0
  Capital share α: 0.30
  Capital K: 125
  Labor L: 100
  
 
 






More capital → wage up, rental down (diminishing returns to capital).
More labor → wage down, rental up.
The shares (\(1-\alpha\) labor, \(\alpha\) capital) never change with K or L — only moving \(\alpha\) re-slices the pie.

title: How a Macro Model Works
text:
A model is a rule that turns exogenous variables (fed in from outside) into endogenous variables (solved inside).

Endogenous = determined by the model — here, the equilibrium price \(P\) and quantity \(Q\).
Exogenous = taken as given — here, buyers’ income and the input price.
Comparative statics = how the solution moves when an exogenous variable changes.




Demand slopes down: \(Q^d = 60 - 10P + 2\cdot\text{Income}\). Higher income shifts it right.
Supply slopes up: \(Q^s = 8P - 2\cdot\text{Input price}\). A costlier input shifts it left.
Equilibrium: the price where \(Q^d = Q^s\) — the market clears.







Try it. Raising income shifts demand right (P and Q both rise). Raising the input price shifts supply left (P rises, Q falls). The grey dot is the baseline.





 
  Buyers' income: 10
  
  Input price: 5
  
  
 
 







Income up → demand shifts right → both P and Q rise.
Input price up → supply shifts left → P rises, Q falls.
The model shows how a shock moves P and Q — not why income itself changed. That needs a bigger model.

title: Loanable Funds & Crowding Out
text:
Think of all saving and borrowing in the economy as one market for a single good — loanable funds — whose “price” is the real interest rate \(r\).

Demand = investment \(I(r)\). Firms borrow to build capital; they borrow less when \(r\) is high, so demand slopes down.
Supply = national saving \(S\) = private \((Y-T-C)\) + public \((T-G)\) = \(Y - C - G\).
Equilibrium: \(r\) adjusts until saving equals investment, \(S = I(r)\).
Crowding out: a bigger deficit (raise \(G\), or cut \(T\)) lowers national saving → \(r\) rises → investment is squeezed.







Try it below. Push the government into deficit and watch \(r\) climb and investment fall. In the baseline, saving slopes up with \(r\); uncheck the box for the vertical-saving case.






  
    Government purchases G: 1500
    
    Taxes T: 1500
    
    Investment-demand shift: 0
    
     Saving slopes up (consumption responds to r) — uncheck for vertical saving
    
  
  
    
  







Run a deficit — raise \(G\) above \(T\). The saving line slides left, \(r\) climbs, and investment falls: crowding out, live.
Shift investment demand (baseline, saving slopes up): \(r\) rises and investment rises.
Uncheck the box for vertical saving and shift demand again: \(r\) rises but \(I^*\) stays put. This is the difference between the two exam cases.

title: Measuring the Economy
text:
GDP = market value of final goods produced: \(Y = C + I + G + NX\).
Nominal vs real: nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP uses base-year prices (so it moves only when quantities move).
GDP deflator \(= \dfrac{\text{Nominal GDP}}{\text{Real GDP}}\times 100\) — a price index for everything the country produces.
Unemployment rate \(u = \dfrac{\text{Unemployed}}{\text{Labor force}}\);   LFPR \(= \dfrac{\text{Labor force}}{\text{Adult population}}\).







Try it. Change the quantity and current price to see nominal, real, and the deflator split apart. Then switch to the labor-market tab.





 
  GDP & the deflator
  Labor market
 
 
  
   One good. Base-year price fixed at $4.
   Quantity produced: 12
   Current price: 5
  
  
   Employed: 180
   Unemployed: 20
   Not in labor force: 50
  
  
 
 






Raise only the current price → nominal GDP rises, real GDP doesn’t → the deflator rises. That’s inflation.
Raise only the quantity → real GDP rises too.
In the labor tab, moving people to “not in labor force” lowers the LFPR but can lower measured unemployment — the denominators differ.

title: Income Distribution & Inequality
text:
The skill premium is the wage ratio of skilled to unskilled workers, \(\omega = w_s/w_u\):
\[\omega = D \cdot \left(\frac{L_u}{L_s}\right)^{1/\sigma}\]

\(L_s/L_u\) = relative supply of skilled workers. More skilled workers (education) → \(\omega\) falls.
\(D\) = relative demand for skill. Skill-biased technical change (SBTC) raises \(D\) → \(\omega\) rises.
\(\sigma\) = how easily firms substitute the two types.







Try it. Educate more workers and the premium falls. Turn up SBTC and it rises — the race between education and technology.





 
  Skilled share of workers: 0.40
  Relative demand for skill D (SBTC): 1.5
  Substitutability σ: 2.0
  
 
 






Slide the skilled share up → the premium falls: expanding education compresses inequality.
Turn up SBTC (D) → the whole curve shifts up: technology favoring skill widens inequality.

title: Large Open Economy & PPP
text:
A large economy’s saving and investment change the world interest rate. Two regions clear together: \(CA_H + CA_{ROW} = 0\), with each \(CA = S - I\) depending on \(r\).

A home fiscal expansion lowers home saving → pushes the world rate up → home investment falls (crowding out).
The adjustment is smaller than in a small economy, because the higher \(r\) pulls saving up and investment down everywhere.



The same good costs the same once converted: \(e = \dfrac{P_{\text{foreign}}}{P_{\text{home}}}\). Higher home inflation → the home currency depreciates one-for-one.






Try it. Left: a home fiscal expansion raises the world rate and crowds out investment. Right: a PPP calculator — change prices to get the exchange rate.





 
  Large open economy
  PPP calculator
 
 
  
   Home fiscal expansion (cuts saving): 0
  
  
   Home price of the good: 3
   Foreign price of the good: 6
  
  
 
 







Home fiscal expansion raises the world rate — unlike a small economy, where \(r^*\) is fixed.
Because \(r\) rises, home investment falls (crowding out).
In the PPP tab, raising the home price lowers \(e\) — the home currency buys less foreign currency.

title: The Fisher Effect & the Money Market
text:
Fisher equation: \(i = r + \pi^e\) — nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation.
Real money demand falls with \(i\). Here \((M/P)^d = \dfrac{Y}{2i}\).
Equilibrium: \(P\) adjusts so \(M/P = \dfrac{Y}{2i}\).
Velocity: \(V = \dfrac{PY}{M} = 2i\).
Ex ante real rate \(= i - \pi^e\); ex post \(= i - \pi\).







Try it. Raise expected inflation: \(i\) rises, people hold less real money, so \(P\) jumps more than the money stock. Watch velocity rise too.





 
  Money supply M: 1000
  Real rate r (%): 2
  Expected inflation pi_e (%): 3
  Real output Y: 1000
  
 
 






Defaults (M=1000, r=2, \(\pi^e\)=3, Y=1000) give i=5, P=10, V=10 — the exam short-answer baseline.
Raise \(\pi^e\): i and V rise, desired real balances fall, and P rises more than M.
The real rate r is set by the real economy; inflation just adds on top (Fisher).
crumbs: The Fisher Effect & the Money Market

title: Quantity Theory & Inflation
text:
The quantity equation is an identity: \(M \cdot V = P \cdot Y\).

\(M\) = money supply, \(V\) = velocity, \(P\) = price level, \(Y\) = real output.
In growth rates (writing \(\Delta\log X\) for the growth rate of \(X\)): \(\Delta\log M + \Delta\log V = \Delta\log P + \Delta\log Y\). With inflation \(\pi = \Delta\log P\),

\[\pi = \Delta\log M + \Delta\log V - \Delta\log Y\]

Quantity theory: if \(V\) is roughly constant (\(\Delta\log V \approx 0\)), then \(\pi = \Delta\log M - \Delta\log Y\) — sustained inflation comes from money growth outrunning real growth.
Classical dichotomy: in the long run money moves only nominal things (P), not real output.







Try it. Money growth above real growth → inflation. Faster output growth absorbs money and lowers inflation. Rising velocity adds to inflation.





 
  Money growth g_M (%): 5
  Output growth g_Y (%): 2
  Velocity growth g_V (%): 0
  
 
 






Set \(g_V = 0\): inflation is exactly \(g_M - g_Y\) — the pure quantity theory.
Faster output growth lowers inflation (more goods absorb the money).
Negative velocity growth pulls inflation down even if money grows.

title: The Costs of Inflation
text:
Shoeleather costs — effort to hold less cash when inflation is high.
Menu costs — the cost of changing posted prices.
Relative-price distortions — staggered price changes misallocate resources.
Redistribution (unexpected inflation) — fixed nominal contracts transfer wealth between borrowers and lenders.
Hyperinflation — all costs balloon; money stops working as a store of value.



A loan sets its nominal rate on expected inflation: \(i = r + \pi^e\). The lender’s realized real return is \(i - \pi\).

If actual \(\pi >\) expected → the borrower gains (repays in cheaper dollars).
If actual \(\pi <\) expected → the lender gains.







Try it. Fix the expected inflation the loan was priced on, then move actual inflation and watch who gains.





 
  Real rate the loan targets r (%): 2
  Expected inflation when signed pi_e (%): 3
  ACTUAL inflation pi (%): 3
  
 
 







Set actual = expected → ex post equals ex ante → no redistribution.
Push actual above expected → the lender’s realized return falls → borrower wins.
Menu, shoeleather, and relative-price costs happen even when inflation is fully expected; redistribution is the extra cost of the surprise.

title: Small Open Economy & the Exchange Rate
text:
With perfect capital mobility, a small country takes the world interest rate as given: \(r = r^*\).

Net exports = net capital outflow: \(NX = S - I = NFI\).
\(r^*\) fixes investment \(I(r^*)\), so it fixes \(S - I\) — hence the trade balance.
The real exchange rate \(\varepsilon\) adjusts so \(NX(\varepsilon) = S - I\).
Tariff: doesn’t touch \(S\) or \(I\) → \(S-I\) fixed → shifts \(NX(\varepsilon)\), so \(\varepsilon\) appreciates but NX is unchanged.







Try it. Left panel: \(r^*\) fixes investment; the gap to saving is net capital outflow. Right panel: the exchange rate slides so net exports equal that gap. A tariff moves \(\varepsilon\) but not NX.





 
  Government purchases G: 1500
  Taxes T: 1500
  Investment-demand shift: 0
  World rate r* (%): 5
  Import tariff (shifts NX): 0
  
 
 






Deficit (G above T): saving slides left, NFI falls, \(\varepsilon\) appreciates.
Lower \(r^*\): investment rises, NFI falls, currency appreciates, NX falls.
Tariff: only the right panel’s NX curve shifts — \(\varepsilon\) rises but the trade balance (NFI) is unchanged. Protectionism can’t fix a trade deficit.

title: What Is Money?
text:
Money = the stock of assets you own and can spend now. It does three jobs: medium of exchange, store of value, unit of account.

Fiat money (dollars) has no intrinsic value; commodity money (gold) does.
Aggregates by liquidity: M0 (currency + reserves) ⊂ M1 (+ checking) ⊂ M2 (+ savings).
Banks lend out deposits, so the base multiplies:

\[M = B \cdot \frac{1+c}{rr+c}\]
\(B\) = monetary base, \(rr\) = reserve ratio, \(c\) = currency-to-deposit ratio. The fraction is the money multiplier.






Try it. An open-market purchase raises the base \(B\). A lower reserve ratio raises the multiplier. Both expand the money supply.





 
  Monetary base B (open-market ops): 500
  Reserve ratio rr: 0.10
  Currency/deposit ratio c: 0.20
  
 
 






A credit-card limit, a check in transit, and an unused credit line are not money — only owned, spendable balances count.
Lower reserve ratio → bigger multiplier → more money from the same base.
The Fed buys bonds to raise B (expand), sells to shrink it.
